Paraguay: after President Peña's fall, his successor fires the head of the Itaipú dam over $182 million placed in the failed Ueno bank

On Wednesday 18 November, Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana fired Justo Zacarías, the Paraguayan-side director of the Itaipú hydroelectric dam, which is shared with Brazil. He is accused of placing more than 180 million dollars in Ueno Bank, which was put under administration on 3 November, a scandal that has already cost President Santiago Peña his job [1][2][3].
Alliana appointed engineer Hugo Osvaldo Zárate Chávez, who has worked at Itaipú for 37 years, to replace him [1][2].

The opposition and dissidents from the ruling Colorado Party had been demanding his departure: Zacarías had authorised two deposits in Ueno Bank, one of 163.8 million dollars, the other in guaraníes, the local currency, worth about 18.3 million dollars [1][2].
The central bank took control of Ueno Bank on 3 November over solvency problems, meaning the bank was no longer able to cover its liabilities [1][2].
In a public letter, Zacarías insists he broke no internal rules and is leaving with a sense of “duty accomplished” [1][4].
The bank's collapse brought down Santiago Peña: the Senate removed him from office a few minutes after his resignation in early November, and Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in [3].

In his first days, Alliana asked all his ministers and senior officials to offer their resignations [5][6]. He promises “fewer words and more results” and wants to compensate the defrauded savers [7][8].
According to La Jornada, the whistleblower in the Ueno affair could take charge of the central bank [5]. Alliana announced further changes in public institutions this week [9].

Key takeaway: in two weeks, a bank failure has brought down a president and is now reaching Itaipú, a binational company shared with Brazil and a pillar of Paraguay's electricity supply [3][1]. The new government wants to show it is cleaning house.

The fact that a state company's money was placed in a fragile bank raises questions about how these funds are overseen. That is why even lawmakers from the ruling party were demanding sanctions [1][2].

Alliana, who belongs to the same Colorado Party as Peña, also has to reassure abroad: he promises to strengthen the “strategic alliance” with the United States [10]. Savers, meanwhile, are waiting to get their money back [8].

This affair is a reminder that a bank failure can quickly turn into a political crisis. In France, your deposits are protected up to a ceiling by a public guarantee, but that is not the case for risky investments: always check who guarantees your money.

Vietnam: in Shenzhen, To Lam and Putin bet on nuclear, gas and wind power, a day after a meeting with Trump

On Wednesday 18 November, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, Vietnamese leader To Lam and Vladimir Putin agreed to deepen their cooperation in energy, from oil and gas to civil nuclear power. The day before, Vietnam's Prime Minister had pressed Donald Trump for a trade deal [1][2][5].
To Lam, General Secretary of the Communist Party and President of Vietnam, met Vladimir Putin on Wednesday 18 November in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of APEC [2][3].
The two countries agreed to deepen their energy cooperation, the Vietnamese government announced, as quoted by Reuters: oil and gas, renewable energy and civil nuclear power were on the agenda [1].
According to Hanoi, the two leaders want to build on their “strengths”, with priority given to traditional and new energy: nuclear, wind and gas-fired power plants [2].

Vladimir Putin proposed coordinating the implementation of “strategic, long-term” projects, especially in energy, according to Vietnam's official news agency [3]. He also offered technology and training in this field [1].
Vietnam is reviving its civil nuclear programme to meet soaring electricity demand, Reuters notes [1].
The day before, on Tuesday 17 November in the Philippines, Vietnam's Prime Minister had met Donald Trump and argued for a “reciprocal” trade deal with the United States [5].
Key takeaway: Vietnam is keeping everyone on side. In two days, its leaders discussed trade with Donald Trump and then energy with Vladimir Putin, on Chinese soil, without picking a camp [1][5].

Energy is the weak spot of a fast-growing economy: to keep up with rising electricity consumption, Hanoi has put civil nuclear power back on the agenda, and Russia, through its nuclear industry, is presenting itself as a partner [1][2].

For Moscow, which is targeted by Western sanctions, these deals in Asia show that it still has partners: in Shenzhen, Putin was surrounded by a crowd of leaders and exchanged a few words with many of them, according to the Kremlin [4].

The same day, Hanoi also agreed with Peru that the two countries would support each other in international forums, including the UN, APEC and the CPTPP, a free trade agreement between Pacific Rim countries [5]. Vietnam is thus lining up support at a time when world trade is fragmenting.

Vietnam has become a major workshop for the clothing, shoes and electronics sold in France. If it runs short of electricity, its factories slow down, and your prices and delivery times suffer. Its deals with Moscow could also complicate its relations with Europe, which sanctions Russia.

news.2026-11-19-ghana-baisse-taux-surpri: Ghana: the central bank surprises everyone by cutting its rate by three points in one go, to 11%

On Wednesday 18 November, the Bank of Ghana cut its policy rate by 300 basis points, or three percentage points, to 11%. Economists polled by Reuters had expected no change, as inflation has been rising for three months, reaching 5.5% in October [1].
The policy rate goes from 14% to 11%, a cut of 300 basis points (one basis point equals 0.01 percentage point) decided by the Bank of Ghana's monetary policy committee in Accra [1].
The decision caught markets off guard: the economists polled by Reuters all expected the rate to stay unchanged [1].

The central bank presents the cut as a “realignment”: market rates, between banks and on government securities, had already fallen below its official rate [1]. In other words, its rate no longer had any grip on actual lending.
The context is delicate: inflation rose for the third month in a row in October, to 5.5%, even though it remains below the central bank's target range [1].
The day before, on Tuesday 17 November, the Accra stock exchange closed almost flat, with its composite index down 0.04% [2].

Key takeaway: Ghana is going for a massive rate cut, three points in one go, even though prices have been rising for three months [1]. It is a rare choice: central banks usually cut rates in small steps, and rather when inflation is falling.

How it works: the policy rate is the price at which the central bank lends to commercial banks. When it falls, banks can lend more cheaply to households and businesses, which supports activity. But if market rates are already lower, the official rate no longer serves as a benchmark: so the Bank of Ghana caught up with the market rather than getting ahead of it [1].

The bet carries a risk: with inflation rising for three months, cutting rates can weaken the currency, the cedi, and make imports more expensive [1]. The central bank evidently believes that inflation, still below its target, gives it room to manoeuvre [1].

For investors, the signal matters: by cutting rates, the Bank of Ghana shows it considers the economy strong enough to loosen the credit squeeze, and Accra's markets, almost flat the day before, will have to digest this surprise [1][2].

The mechanism is the same as in France: when the ECB cuts rates, your mortgage gets cheaper, but your savings account earns less. And if you have “emerging markets” funds in your life insurance policy, this kind of surprise moves the African bonds they hold.

Alstom falls to its lowest since 2005: after €954 million in losses, the market expects to be asked for more money

On Wednesday 18 November, Alstom shares lost 7.15% in Paris and hit their lowest intraday level since May 2005. The train maker lost 954 million euros in six months and wants to cut its debt by 2 billion: analysts fear a capital increase [1][2][3][5][6].

On the evening of 17 November, the train maker reported a net loss of 954 million euros for the first half of its 2026-2027 financial year (April to September), compared with a profit of 220 million a year earlier [2][3].

The main cause: its Coradia Max regional trains sold in Germany. About two thirds of the German margin losses come from six contracts, and the first certification is now not expected before March 2028 at the earliest [3]. Production fell 8%, to 1,860 cars [3].

Net debt climbed to about 1.1 billion euros at the end of September, compared with about 404 million at the end of March [1]. Alstom is aiming for about 2 billion euros of deleveraging by September 2027, through asset sales and “equity or quasi-equity financing” [3][4][5].
On the stock market, the shares fell more than 9% at the start of trading, to 9.08 euros, their lowest since May 2005 according to Reuters, before closing down 7.15% [1][6].

Banks are reading between the lines: Deutsche Bank believes asset sales will be limited and expects a capital increase to cover most of the plan; Citi puts the equity portion at 1.5 billion euros [5][7].

Martin Sion, the chief executive, called the results “unsatisfactory” and promised this would be “the last delay” for the Coradia Max [3]. The group is reviewing its factories, its organisation and its product range [1][3].

Key takeaway: Alstom, France's rail champion and one of the world's major train makers, is caught in a vicious circle. Poorly managed contracts are burning through its cash, its debt is swelling, and it needs to find fresh money to keep its credit rating [1][3].

This is the third shock of the year. On 17 April, the shares lost about 30% when the group dropped its three-year cash target [10]. On 2 November came a new warning: Alstom forecast negative cash flow of 1.5 billion euros for the financial year, and the shares fell 28%; by then they had lost 54% since January [11].

The group is determined to stay “investment grade”, the club of borrowers considered safe [4]. Losing that status would make its borrowing more expensive and could hamper its bids for tenders, where customers demand financial guarantees.

For European industry, the stakes go beyond the stock market: Alstom has launched a review of its production sites and organisation, with decisions expected by the end of the year [3]. In 2024, its major shareholders included the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec and Bpifrance, the French public investment bank [9].

If you hold Alstom shares or a fund that contains them, a capital increase could dilute your stake if you don't take part. More broadly, train delivery delays are also felt on the platforms: regions and operators are waiting for their trains, in Germany as in France.

How it works: why a capital increase pushes the share price down

A company with too much debt can ask its shareholders for money by creating new shares: this is a capital increase. The cake (the company) stays the same, but it is cut into more slices, so each share represents a little less: this is called dilution. To attract buyers, the new shares are sold below the market price: in 2024, Alstom offered them at 13 euros, a discount of about 28.6% [9]. With a “preferential subscription right”, each shareholder receives rights that let them buy first to keep their stake, or sell those rights on [5][9]. Investors often sell before the announcement, which pushes the share price down as soon as the scenario becomes likely [5][7].
Precedents: Alstom, twenty years of rescues and warnings

On the brink of bankruptcy, Alstom is rescued by the French state: with Brussels' approval in July 2004, the state takes 21% of the capital for 720 million euros and provides 2.8 billion euros in loans and its guarantee [8].
The bet paid off: in June 2006, the state sold its stake to Bouygues for 2 billion euros, with a capital gain of 1.26 billion [8].
5 October 2023
Alstom lowers its cash flow target, now expected to be negative by 500 to 750 million euros: the shares plunge 37.5%, to 13.3 euros, their worst session in more than 20 years [12].
Seven months later, in May 2024, Alstom presented a 2 billion euro deleveraging plan [9].
May-June 2024
To complete this plan, Alstom raises 1 billion euros in new shares at 13 euros each, with the backing of the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec (17.4% of the capital) and Bpifrance (7.5%) [9].
The deleveraging had reassured investors, but two years later the debt is rising again and the same remedy is back on the table [1][5].
17 April 2026
Alstom abandons its target of more than 1.5 billion euros in cash flow over three years: the shares lose about 30% [10].
The start of a dark year, followed by the 28% drop on 2 November [11].

The Mexican peso has its worst session since 2024: the Fed is preparing new rate hikes and investors are pulling out of emerging-market currencies

On Wednesday 18 November, the Mexican peso lost 2.26% against the dollar, to 18.84 pesos, its steepest fall since June 2024. The cause: the minutes of the US Federal Reserve, in which almost all officials consider further rate hikes likely [1][3][6].

The dollar ended at 18.84 pesos according to data from the Bank of Mexico (Banxico), a 2.26% depreciation of the peso, according to El Financiero [1]. The broker Monex, quoted by Expansión, measures a 2.43% fall, to 18.8643 pesos [2].

During the session, the peso fell as low as 18.88 pesos to the dollar, a 2.5% loss according to Bloomberg Línea [4], and Publimetro notes a peak of 18.93 [5]. The peso ended the day as the worst-performing currency of the day [5].

The trigger: the minutes of the Fed's 27-28 October meeting, published on Wednesday. “Almost all” participants judged that a further increase in the target range for policy rates “would likely be appropriate” to bring inflation back to 2% [6].

In October, the Fed had held its rates between 3.75% and 4% by 10 votes to 2, with Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack already favouring a quarter-point hike; a few members raised the possibility of a bigger move in December if inflation disappoints [7].
According to Publimetro, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said a half-point hike should be considered at the 9 December meeting [5].

Monex attributes the fall to expectations of a tougher Fed and to the unwinding of bets that profited from high yields on emerging-market currencies [2]. In Brazil, the São Paulo stock exchange lost 1.25% [9].

Key takeaway: part of the buying of pesos relied on the “carry trade”, a bet that consists of borrowing in a low-interest currency to invest in a high-interest one. When the rate gap narrows, these bets are unwound all at once, and the currency falls [2].

The gap is shrinking on both sides. In Washington, the Fed is heading towards hikes. In Mexico City, Banxico surprised on 5 November by cutting its rate to 6.25%, by three votes to two [8][10]. According to the bank UBS, quoted by Expansión, 500 basis points (5 percentage points) of cumulative cuts by Banxico have eroded the peso's advantage [2].

A weaker peso makes what Mexico imports in dollars more expensive, which can reignite inflation, and increases the burden of dollar-denominated debt. On the other hand, it makes Mexican products sold in the United States cheaper, and therefore more competitive.
The issue goes beyond Mexico: a dollar rising with US rates weighs on all emerging-market currencies, from Indonesia to Brazil [2][9].

For you, the direct effect is limited, but the mechanism matters: when US rates rise faster than elsewhere, the dollar strengthens against many currencies. And if you have an “emerging markets” fund in your life insurance policy or your PEA (French equity savings plan), this kind of session shows its weak spot.

How it works: the “carry trade”, or why a currency collapses when US rates rise

An investor borrows money where it is cheap, then invests it where it earns more, for example in Mexican bonds. As long as the rate gap is wide and the currency is stable, they pocket the difference. But if US rates rise while Mexico's fall, the gain melts away [2]. Investors then sell their pesos to buy back dollars, all at the same time: demand for pesos falls, and so does its price. That drop in turn makes latecomers lose money, and they sell too: this is the snowball effect of “unwinding” [2].

As on Wednesday, a sharp fall can wipe out months of currency gains in a single day [3].

Measurements differ depending on the closing time used, but all of them place Wednesday among the worst sessions in more than a year [2][3].
5 November 2026
Against most forecasts, Banxico cuts its rate by a quarter point, to 6.25%, by three votes to two, with Jonathan Heath and Galia Borja voting against [8][10].
Less than two weeks later, the narrower rate gap with the United States is taking its toll on the exchange rate [2][8].

news.2026-11-19-indonesie-hausse-taux-ro: Indonesia: to rescue the rupiah from a record low, the central bank unexpectedly raises rates to 6%

On Wednesday 18 November, Bank Indonesia raised its policy rate by a quarter point, to 6%, an unexpected decision to defend the rupiah, which fell the day before to 18,285 to the dollar, its all-time low. The currency barely reacted [1][2].
At the end of its 17-18 November meeting, Bank Indonesia (BI) raised its policy rate, the BI-Rate, by 0.25 point, to 6% [1][2]. The deposit rate rises to 5.25% and the lending rate to 6.75% [2][3].
According to Reuters, the decision was unexpected and revives a cycle of hikes: 125 basis points (1.25 points) in total since May [1].
